# Pick and configure the RMW

<!-- type: tutorial · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Add a second node](add-a-second-node.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: chapter status -->
> **Status:** this chapter runs on [`nros-board-mps2-an385`](../reference/boards/mps2-an385.md): Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry; [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED chapter status -->

Every nano-ros image talks to ROS 2 through one RMW, the ROS middleware
layer: zenoh, Cyclone DDS or XRCE-DDS. In this chapter you see which one the
project uses and what it needs beside the board, then reconfigure it: the
board leaves its serial port and reaches its zenoh router over its emulated
Ethernet instead. At the end, `nros run` prints

```text
nros run: starting the zenoh router on tcp/127.0.0.1:7447
```

where it used to name a serial device, the board prints its own network
address, and `ros2 topic echo` still receives every message. You also know
what changing to the other two RMWs takes, and when you would.

Run every step from the root of `sensor_ws`.

## Find the project's RMW

```bash probe=410 track=installed variant=qemu
grep -n 'rmw\|locator' src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml
```

```text
7:rmw = "zenoh"
23:locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"
```

Two lines decide how the project reaches ROS 2. `rmw = "zenoh"` in
`[system]` picks the middleware for every image of the bringup. `locator`,
in `[image.baremetal]`, says where this image finds its zenoh router: on
UART 0, at 115,200 baud. The line numbers depend on the comments the scaffold
wrote; the two lines are what matter.

The RMW is chosen when the image is built, not when it starts. ROS 2 reads
`RMW_IMPLEMENTATION` when a process starts and loads that middleware's shared
library; a microcontroller has no shared libraries to load and no environment
to read. So the build links the chosen backend into the image, and only that
one: an image built for zenoh contains no DDS code at all. Changing the RMW
means editing the `rmw` line and building again.

## Compare the three backends

All three carry topics, services and actions between a nano-ros image and
ROS 2. They differ in what has to run beside your image, and in what the
image needs from its board:

| | zenoh | Cyclone DDS | XRCE-DDS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runs beside the image | ROS 2's zenoh router, `rmw_zenohd` | nothing | the Micro XRCE-DDS Agent, `MicroXRCEAgent` |
| ROS 2 side | `rmw_zenoh_cpp` | `rmw_cyclonedds_cpp`, directly | any DDS RMW, through the agent |
| Links | serial, TCP, UDP | UDP, multicast discovery | serial, UDP, TCP |
| Board needs (planning numbers) | about 16 KB RAM, 100 KB flash | a heap, about 32 KB RAM, 150 KB flash, an IP stack with IGMP | about 3 KB RAM, 75 KB flash |
| `rmw =` | `"zenoh"` | `"cyclonedds"` | `"xrce"` |

The RAM and flash figures are order-of-magnitude planning numbers, not
measurements of your image; chapter 8 measures this project's. The
[RMW feature matrix](../reference/matrices/rmw-feature-matrix.md) lists what
each backend supports, generated from the backends' sources: in short, all
three do publish and subscribe, services and status events, and they differ
in the less common features, such as graph introspection and zero-copy loans.

How to choose:

- **zenoh** when the board is small, when its only link to the host is a
  serial port, or when the ROS 2 side already runs `rmw_zenoh_cpp`. It needs
  the router, and the router comes from ROS 2, so a machine with ROS 2
  installed already has it.
- **Cyclone DDS** when the target has an operating system with a network
  stack, such as the Linux host or an RTOS board with Ethernet, and you want
  nothing running beside it. A stock ROS 2 node using `rmw_cyclonedds_cpp`
  sees it directly, with the same wire protocol and the same discovery.
- **XRCE-DDS** when RAM is the tightest constraint, or when the device joins a
  micro-ROS or DDS deployment that already runs an agent. The device does no
  discovery of its own; if the agent stops, the device loses all
  connectivity.

On this board the choice is made for you: the board support registry
verifies the MPS2-AN385 bare-metal image with zenoh, which is why chapter 1
provisioned `--rmw zenoh`. Chapter 9 runs the same project on the Linux host,
where Cyclone DDS runs too.

[How nano-ros differs from ROS 2](../background/differences-from-ros2.md#how-each-backend-reaches-ros-2)
explains how each backend reaches the ROS 2 graph, and what happens when the
router, the agent or a peer goes away.

## Move the board onto its network

Serial came first because it is the simplest link a board has: two wires,
no addresses, nothing to configure. The MPS2-AN385 also has an Ethernet
controller, and QEMU connects it to a private network on your host, in which
your host is `10.0.2.2` and the board is `10.0.2.15`. Change the image's
`locator` to dial the router over TCP on that network:

```toml
[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7447"
```

Edit the line in `src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml` by hand, or run:

```bash probe=420 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i 's#^locator = .*#locator = "tcp/10.0.2.2:7447"#' src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml
```

A zenoh locator is `<link>/<address>`: `serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200` was
the board's first serial port, and `tcp/10.0.2.2:7447` is TCP to port 7447 of
the host, the zenoh router's usual port. Nothing else changes. The node
packages do not name a link, and the board's own description already says
which network devices it has and how its network stack is built.

## Run it over the network

```bash probe=430 probe-run=900 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run --expect 'I heard:'
```

```text probe-expect=430 variant=qemu
nros run: starting the zenoh router on tcp/127.0.0.1:7447
I heard: [Hello World: 1]
```

The image is rebuilt with the board's network stack in place of its serial
link, then boots. A Rust project's console, trimmed:

```text
nros run: starting the zenoh router on tcp/127.0.0.1:7447

Initializing LAN9118 Ethernet...
  MAC: 02:00:00:00:00:00

Creating network interface...
  IP: 10.0.2.15
Ethernet ready.

Application setup complete — entering spin loop.
[INFO] sensor_node: [    1.338059] Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
[INFO] monitor_node: [    1.418620] I heard: [Hello World: 1]
nros run: matched after 1.7 s: [INFO] monitor_node: [    1.418620] I heard: [Hello World: 1]
```

Compare it with chapter 3's run. The board now brings up the LAN9118
Ethernet controller and takes the address `10.0.2.15`, where it used to bring
up its serial port. `nros run` read the new locator and started the router
listening on TCP port 7447 of your host's loopback address, because QEMU's
network delivers `10.0.2.2` to your host's loopback. Before, it started the
router on the serial device QEMU created, after QEMU had created it.

`nros run` starts the router only when the image needs one and the address
is this host's. With `--router none` it starts nothing, and with
`--router tcp/<host>:<port>` it uses a router you already run elsewhere.

## See it in ROS 2

The ROS 2 side has not changed: it reaches the same router, which now talks
to the board over TCP. Start the board in one terminal:

```bash probe=440 probe-run=600 probe-keep track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run
```

```text probe-expect=440 variant=qemu
Publishing: 'Hello World:
```

and, in a second terminal, the same command as in chapter 1:

```bash probe=445 probe-run=120 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

```text probe-expect=445 variant=qemu
data: 'Hello World:
```

Press Ctrl-C in both terminals when you have seen enough. The rest of the
Tutorial keeps the board on its network.

## What switching the RMW takes

On a board that supports more than one backend, switching is two edits and a
provisioning step. This board's image stays on zenoh, so read this section
rather than run it; [Switch the RMW per image](../guide/rmw/switch-the-rmw-per-image.md)
is the full procedure.

1. **Provision the backend for the board:**
   `nros setup <board> --rmw cyclonedds` (or `--rmw xrce`) fetches what that
   backend needs, as chapter 1's `--rmw zenoh` did for zenoh.
2. **Change the `rmw` line.** In `[system]`, it changes every image of the
   bringup. Set inside one `[image.*]` table, it changes that image only, so
   one bringup can build its board image with zenoh and its host image with
   Cyclone DDS:

   ```toml
   [image.linux]
   board = "linux"
   rmw = "cyclonedds"
   ```

3. **Change the link to the backend's.** Cyclone DDS needs no locator: it
   finds its peers by multicast on the network, and its domain is
   `[system] domain_id`. XRCE-DDS dials its agent, so its `locator` names the
   agent's address and port, such as `udp/10.0.2.2:2018`, and `nros run`
   starts `MicroXRCEAgent` on that port the way it starts the zenoh router.

Then `nros run` again. The node packages do not change for any of the three:
the same code publishes over each, because the backend sits below the client
library the nodes call.

## What just happened

You configured the project's **RMW in use**: the backend linked into the
image, and the link it uses to reach whatever runs beside it.

Three facts carry over to every board and every later chapter:

- **The RMW is a build-time choice, per image.** The `rmw` line picks it, in
  `[system]` for every image or in one `[image.*]` for that image. The build
  links that backend alone. There is no `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION` switch on an
  embedded target, and the image cannot change its backend after it is
  built.
- **Each backend has its own peer beside the image.** zenoh needs a router,
  XRCE-DDS an agent, and Cyclone DDS nothing but a network that carries
  multicast. `nros run` starts the router or the agent when the image's link
  points at your host, which is why the project has never needed you to
  start one by hand.
- **The link is configuration, not code.** The board went from a serial
  port to Ethernet by one `locator` line. Serial needs nothing but a port and
  a baud rate, which makes it the first link to try on any new board; a
  network needs addresses, which the board's description and the image
  supply. WiFi is deferred: no chapter of this book uses it yet.

## Design background

Choosing the backend at build time follows
[RFC-0031](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0031-rmw-selection-and-lowering.md);
using ROS 2's own router follows
[RFC-0075](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0075-zenoh-router-provenance-and-the-unstable-seam.md);
`nros run` starting it follows
[RFC-0118](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0118-target-execution-model.md)
D8. RMW use before RMW implementation is
[RFC-0124](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0124-book-user-guide-organization.md)
D5.
